source.title: Safety vs. Performance: How Multi-Objective Learning Reduces Barriers to Market Entry
source.authors: Meena Jagadeesan; Michael I. Jordan; Jacob Steinhardt

record.tranche_reason: The paper derives scaling laws for multi-objective high-dimensional linear regression and finds that their exponents change across dataset-size regimes, refining the claim that scaling follows one stable power law. This is a theoretical analysis, not an empirical test on language models.
record.gate_note: The paper does not measure language-model pretraining loss or sweep model parameters, tokens, or compute. Its own results are theoretical scaling laws for a linear-regression model; cited language-model scaling exponents are context, not new results. Market-entry threshold results are not rows because they do not measure the loss scaling behavior in the claim.
record.test_reason: This is a theoretical market-entry paper. It takes empirical power-law scaling as a modelling premise, citing Kaplan and Hoffmann and plugging in ν = 0.34 for illustration. Its own scaling results are analytic Θ-rates for the deterministic equivalent of optimally regularized ridge regression under assumed power-law spectra. It measures no language, image, video, fine-tuned or transfer model. No result bears on any version as a behaviour of the kind of system the versions name. The derived multi-regime ('slowing') rates are a related theoretical construct, recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right but misplaces the emphasis. The main conclusion is about markets: safety pressure on incumbents lets entrants enter with much less data, sublinear in the incumbent's data or even finite. The multi-objective scaling law, slowing as N grows because regularization must avoid overfitting alternate-labelled data, is presented as a technical tool 'of independent interest'.
record.recipe_differences: The paper develops a theoretical random-matrix and ridge-regression analysis with optimally tuned regularization, rather than empirically fitting neural language-model loss against parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The derived exponents vary with dataset-size regime, the primary-objective data fraction α, correlation ρ, and power-law exponents γ and δ; the excess-loss result also depends on using excess loss rather than loss.

fits_no_version.finding: In multi-objective ridge regression (fraction 1−α labelled by an alternate linear target), the optimally regularized loss exponent falls with N. It goes from ν to ν/(ν+1) to 0 for loss, and to ν′/(ν′+1) for excess loss. This is derived analytically under assumed power-law spectra, with P = ∞.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Theoretical: mixing training data from conflicting objectives yields broken power-law data scaling, slowing as dataset size grows, in high-dimensional linear regression.

record.problems: The results rely on high-dimensional linear-regression and power-law assumptions, including P → ∞. The authors state that they do not control the error of the deterministic equivalent relative to actual loss, and note simplifying choices in the safety-loss definition. There are no empirical language-model results or uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: Market-entry threshold results in Theorems 1, 4, 5, 42, 47, and 49 concern required entrant data rather than the loss scaling behavior named by the versions. Cited language-model scaling results are not the paper's own results.

untested.parts: No measured pretraining loss of any language model versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No image, video, repeated-data, fine-tuning or transfer models are trained or measured. Only a stylized ridge-regression theory is analysed.
No empirical fits, fitting-method or parameter-counting comparisons, and no measured curve-bending in real models.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'tests/T5' and its V5 and V7 labels are rejected. Ridge regression is not the kind of system the versions name, and the results are analytic Θ-rates of a deterministic equivalent, not measurements. The ν = 0.34 values are illustrations from Hoffmann et al., not new results. The market-entry theorems are correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss measurements on language models or sweeps over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No fitted small-run forecasts compared with larger language-model runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between model parameters and training tokens.
No comparisons of depth, width, or other architecture details.
The study analyzes a theoretical multi-objective linear-regression setting only; it does not test image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer on actual models.

The paper shows dependence on objective mixture and dataset-size regime in its theoretical setting, but does not compare empirical fitting methods, parameter-counting conventions, language-model training schedules, or published language-model exponents.

rows.subject: multi-objective high-dimensional linear regression (ridge regression)
rows.operation_detail: Derives the optimally regularized scaling law for loss on the primary linear objective as dataset size N varies.

conditions.value: α ≥ 0.5 of data labelled by the primary objective; 1−α by the alternate objective
power-law eigenvalues and alignment coefficients; γ, δ > 0; ρ ∈ [0,1); ν = min(2(1+γ), δ+γ)

rows.measure: Expected primary-objective loss under optimal regularization
rows.baseline: Single-objective scaling exponent ν; the paper says this regime has the same exponent as the single-objective setting.
rows.note: Analytical asymptotic result, not an empirical model measurement.
rows.check: Analytic Θ-rate for ridge regression's deterministic-equivalent loss (Corollary 8, regime 1). It is not a measurement of a neural model's loss, so it cannot bear on V5 or V7.

rows.measure: Expected primary-objective loss under optimal regularization
rows.baseline: First-regime exponent ν; the paper states the second-regime exponent is smaller.
rows.note: The text gives ν = 0.34 as an illustrative language-model exponent and says the second-regime exponent is approximately 0.25. This is an illustration using a cited estimate, not a new language-model result.
rows.check: Analytic rate for a toy linear model (Corollary 8, regime 2). The ≈0.25 figure only illustrates a cited Hoffmann exponent and is not a measured result.

rows.measure: Expected primary-objective loss under optimal regularization
rows.value: Θ((1−α)^2(1−ρ)); exponent with respect to N is 0, and further data improves loss only through constants.
rows.note: The result describes a plateau in loss, up to constants, in the large-N regime.
rows.check: Analytic plateau of a toy linear model (Corollary 8, regime 3). It shows no curve-bending in any real trained model.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The derived laws have dataset-size-dependent exponents and can plateau for loss, so the form and rate need qualification in this setting; see r1–r6.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Theorems 2 and 3 under their stated mixture and power-law assumptions
reader_labels.reason: The scaling exponent changes across dataset-size regimes, and the results depend on mixture proportion and on whether loss or excess loss is measured; see r1–r6.
